title: Majestic Sacrifices
reviewNotes: Three branches start in the seven-piece pawn ending at 65s with White Kg5 and Black Kd4, Black to move. The encoded continuations are explicitly independent representative replies: Ke4 followed by king activation, gxh6+, capture of g3 and f-pawn promotion wins for Black. Immediate g6 draws; h6+ actually loses for Black. Practice side is Black. Earlier larger sacrifices and the separate later pawn mate remain source context.
transcript: Knight G3 check is a brilliant sacrifice that gives up the knight completely. And of course the knight has to be captured because if you don't, this is just going to pick up the queen on the next move. But okay, so what? White can just take the knight and now has a queen and a bishop for a bishop and a rook and is completely winning, right? Well, not exactly. Black has a brilliant sequence that is going to allow him to win this game. And that sequence starts with the majestic bishop to F3. Another beautiful sacrifice and another fork of the queen and king, which means that the bishop has to be taken once again. And now it seems like all hope is lost. But notice that the two pieces sacrificed have opened up a path for the rook to check the white king. And indeed, [music] black continues king to D4. This opens up a check on the king and white has to reply. Blocking the check with the bishop would make no sense after rook takes A5. This is a fork attacking the queen and king again. And after the queen takes, this is a winning king and pawn end game and black is going to win. But white shouldn't be worried about this check. He can just play king to G4 and now be completely sheltered [music] from any further checks. Or at least it seems like it. But there are more checks with pawn to H5. The rook covers the entire fifth rank and defends the pawn, which means that the only legal move is king to F4. And now some of you might notice that we can actually win the queen by force with E5 check. But this is a mistake because after the king moves and after we do give the check, white is going to sacrifice the queen like this, forcing us to give up the rook. And actually with the bishop left, it is white that is playing for an advantage. So it seems like black has run out of all resources and white is simply going to win. But we have not run out of checks quite yet. There is pawn to G5, a move that seems mysterious. Doesn't this still lose more material? But, you see, chess is a very concrete game, and material is only one of many ways to decide who is better in a given position. And in fact, the only way for black to win this position is to sacrifice the last piece that he has with the rook to F5. The king is almost checkmated, so the rook has to be taken by the bishop. [music] And now, with only two pawns left and the white pieces betraying their own king, pawn to E5 is checkmate.
